AltText: Tinder-dry purple moor-grass (Molinia caerulea) by Fur Tor on Dartomoor, four days before a large wildlife broke out nearby.
Title: Tinder
Description:
I had the news on in the background while I was making dinner yesterday, and there was a report airing about the fire in Stourbridge which destroyed nineteen homes, when the emergency alert came through to my phone. Naturally, my first thought was OH NO THERE’S A MASSIVE WILDFIRE IN THE IMMEDIATE VICINITY. Luckily, this was not the case, so my dinner did not go cold. Or get incinerated.

This purple moor-grass near where I camped by Fur Tor last year was tinder-dry after weeks of little or no rain. That was just a taster for the drought now gripping the UK. Four days later, a wildfire started about a mile from where I took this photo, and destroyed a large area of moorland. At the time, the area destroyed was reported as fifty square kilometres. Looking again now, I see this was revised to five square kilometres, which is quite an error to make.

This was my second trip to Dartmoor to photograph the temperate rainforests. Neither trip was particularly successful on that front, since on both occasions a lack of rain before and during my visit had left them looking quite desiccated and miserable. I hate to think what they are looking like now. Temperate rainforest is such a rare habitat that many people who have lived their whole lives in Britain don’t know we have it, or perhaps even that it exists anywhere. On Wednesday, before the eclipse, I was walking along the River Darent and saw an information board describing chalk streams as “England’s rainforests”, one of several such epithets which Guy Shrubsole laments in The Lost Rainforests of Britain, noting that “Britain’s rainforests are ‘our rainforests’”.

Luckily, it seems that there have been no wildfires on Dartmoor yet this year, but it will be a while before we are out of the danger zone.
